triage.name: Dizziness and Vertigo
triage.reason: Very common undifferentiated symptom with a broad differential (BPPV, vestibular neuritis, central causes) that students work through by history, exam maneuvers and imaging.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common with increasing age; the risk roughly doubles each decade after age 40
Women account for a larger share of clinic visits for dizziness, especially in middle age

risk_factors.text: Prior head injury or ear surgery

social_history: Low fluid intake or heavy alcohol use
exposures: Prolonged bed rest or recent hospitalization
Hot weather or exertion with poor hydration

chief_complaints.text: I feel lightheaded when I stand up
I feel unsteady on my feet
I get woozy when I turn my head

hpi.onset: Varies by cause: sudden over seconds to minutes with BPPV or vestibular neuritis, or gradual over days to weeks with medication effects or deconditioning
hpi.duration: Episodes may last seconds (BPPV), minutes to hours (Meniere's or migraine), or days (vestibular neuritis)
hpi.progression: Often intermittent and recurrent; may improve spontaneously or persist until the underlying cause is treated
hpi.location: Felt in the head or as a whole-body sensation; not localized to one side
hpi.quality: Spinning or whirling sensation, or a floating, lightheaded, woozy feeling
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; can be disabling during attacks and may interfere with walking or driving
hpi.timing: Often triggered by specific movements or positions; may be constant or episodic

associated_symptoms.text: Feeling of fullness in the ear

pertinent_negatives: Sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body

positives.text: Feeling warm or sweaty during episodes

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with falls, confusion, or generalized weakness rather than a clear spinning sensation; multiple causes often coexist (medications, orthostasis, vestibular loss, neuropathy).
Young children may not describe vertigo; they present with irritability, clinging, unsteady gait, or vomiting, and the differential includes migraine equivalents and inner ear infections.
Dizziness is common due to physiologic changes; orthostatic hypotension, anemia, and hyperemesis must be considered, and medication choices are limited.
Autonomic neuropathy can cause orthostatic dizziness, and hypoglycemia can present with lightheadedness and sweating.
Higher risk of central nervous system infections or tumors presenting with dizziness, and symptoms may be atypical or blunted.

general.moderate: Uncomfortable, cautious with movement, mild unsteadiness
general.severe: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, needs support to sit or stand, may vomit
general.critical: Toxic or neurologically impaired, unable to stand or protect airway, focal deficits

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure and heart rate supine, then after standing for 1 and 3 minutes
findings.finding: Drop in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mm Hg or diastolic of at least 10 mm Hg, or heart rate rise over 30 bpm, with symptoms

findings.maneuver: With the patient seated, turn the head 45 degrees to one side and rapidly lay them back with the head hanging 20 degrees below horizontal; observe eyes for nystagmus and ask about vertigo
findings.finding: Brief latency (seconds), upbeat-torsional nystagmus lasting under a minute, with reproduction of vertigo, that fatigues on repeat testing

findings.maneuver: With the patient supine, turn the head quickly to one side, then the other, and observe for nystagmus
findings.finding: Positional nystagmus with vertigo, consistent with horizontal canal involvement

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to fixate on your nose, grasp the head, and turn it quickly about 15 degrees to each side
findings.finding: Corrective saccade after the head turn, indicating a unilateral peripheral vestibular deficit

findings.maneuver: Observe the eyes in primary gaze and with gaze held to each side
findings.finding: Spontaneous horizontal nystagmus that is unidirectional and suppressed by visual fixation, suggesting peripheral cause

findings.maneuver: Cover one eye, then the other, and observe for vertical corrective movement
findings.finding: Vertical skew deviation, suggesting a central cause

findings.maneuver: Rub fingers near each ear or perform bedside whisper test
findings.finding: Asymmetric or unilateral hearing loss

findings.maneuver: Inspect the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane with an otoscope
findings.finding: Normal canal and intact, mobile tympanic membrane without effusion or vesicles

findings.maneuver: Test cranial nerves II through XII, including extraocular movements, facial symmetry, palate elevation, and tongue movement
findings.finding: Normal cranial nerve examination without diplopia, facial droop, dysarthria, or dysphagia

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to touch your finger and then their nose with eyes open and closed
findings.finding: No limb dysmetria or intention tremor

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to stand with feet together and arms at sides, first with eyes open then closed
findings.finding: Increased sway or fall with eyes closed, suggesting proprioceptive or vestibular loss

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient walking, including tandem gait if safe
findings.finding: Wide-based, unsteady, or veering gait; inability to tandem walk

findings.maneuver: Test strength in all four extremities
findings.finding: Normal, symmetric strength without drift

findings.maneuver: Test light touch, pinprick, and vibration in the extremities
findings.finding: Normal sensation without a sensory level or stocking-glove loss

findings.maneuver: Test deep tendon reflexes at the biceps, brachioradialis, patella, and Achilles
findings.finding: Normal, symmetric reflexes without pathologic reflexes

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart in the standard positions
findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm or murmur suggesting arrhythmia or valvular disease
Bruit suggesting carotid stenosis or vertebrobasilar disease

findings.maneuver: Assess neck flexibility and meningeal signs
findings.finding: Nuchal rigidity or positive Brudzinski/Kernig signs
Normal mental status without confusion or disorientation

labs.caveat: Anemia causes lightheadedness and unsteadiness rather than true spinning vertigo; a low value points away from a vestibular cause.
Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of lightheadedness, sweating and confusion; check it at the bedside in any patient on insulin or a sulfonylurea.
Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism can cause dizziness; a suppressed TSH with high free T4 suggests hyperthyroidism.
Hyponatremia from thiazides or SIADH causes confusion, unsteadiness and lightheadedness.
Elevated creatinine suggests dehydration or kidney injury, which can cause orthostatic dizziness and limits medication choices.
A BUN-to-creatinine ratio above 20 supports dehydration as a contributor to orthostatic dizziness.
Check in anyone of childbearing age before imaging or medication changes; a positive result changes the differential and the imaging plan.
A high white count with fever and neck stiffness raises concern for meningitis or a central nervous system infection.
Nonspecific; a marked rise with fever suggests infection such as meningitis or mastoiditis.
Very high values in an older adult with headache and jaw claudication suggest giant cell arteritis.
Deficiency causes sensory ataxia and unsteadiness, especially in older adults and after gastric surgery.
Poorly controlled diabetes raises the odds of autonomic neuropathy causing orthostatic dizziness.

findings.finding: Atrial fibrillation with irregularly irregular ventricular response
Sinus bradycardia
Second- or third-degree atrioventricular block
Tachycardia (sinus or supraventricular)
ST-segment elevation or depression suggesting myocardial ischemia
Prolonged QT interval

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected central cause such as stroke, mass, or demyelination; better than CT for the posterior fossa

findings.text: Acute infarction in the cerebellum, brainstem, or thalamus
Cerebellar atrophy or small vessel ischemic changes

imaging.preferred_when: Acute setting when MRI is unavailable or the patient is unstable; screens for hemorrhage and large masses

findings.text: CT is often normal in acute posterior circulation stroke

imaging.study: CT angiography of the head and neck
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected vertebrobasilar dissection, occlusion, or stenosis

findings.text: Vertebral or basilar artery stenosis or occlusion
Vertebral artery dissection with intramural hematoma or luminal irregularity

imaging.study: MRI of the internal auditory canals with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, or suspected retrocochlear lesion

findings.text: Enhancing mass in the cerebellopontine angle or internal auditory canal (vestibular schwannoma)
Enhancement of the vestibular nerve (labyrinthitis or neuritis)

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected carotid stenosis in a patient with transient neurologic symptoms

findings.text: Hemodynamically significant internal carotid artery stenosis

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected cardiac source of embolus or structural heart disease with syncope or dizziness

findings.text: Degenerative changes of the cervical spine

initial.why: Bedside glucose is the fastest way to catch hypoglycemia as a reversible cause of lightheadedness
Screens for anemia, which causes lightheadedness and unsteadiness
Checks sodium, glucose, and kidney function; dehydration and electrolyte problems are common contributors
Thyroid disease is a treatable cause of dizziness and unsteadiness
Looks for arrhythmia, bradycardia, or ischemia as a cardiac cause
Rules out pregnancy before imaging or medication changes

confirmatory.test: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Best test for a central cause such as stroke, mass, or demyelination when the history or exam suggests it
confirmatory.only_if: central cause is suspected (focal neurologic findings, new severe headache, inability to walk, vascular risk factors, or persistent vertigo with nystagmus that does not fit a peripheral pattern)

confirmatory.why: Rapid screen for hemorrhage or mass when MRI is unavailable or the patient is unstable
confirmatory.only_if: acute presentation with red flags and MRI is not immediately available

supporting.why: Identifies diabetes that may have caused autonomic neuropathy
Deficiency causes sensory ataxia and unsteadiness
supporting.only_if: older adult, vegan, or prior gastric surgery

supporting.why: Supports an inflammatory or infectious process
Very high values raise concern for giant cell arteritis
supporting.only_if: older adult with headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms

supporting.test: MRI of the internal auditory canals with and without contrast
CT angiography of the head and neck
supporting.only_if: suspected dissection or posterior circulation ischemia
transient neurologic symptoms in a vascular territory

supporting.why: Looks for a cardiac source of embolus or structural disease
supporting.only_if: syncope, murmur, or suspected cardioembolic source

not_indicated.why: Not useful in dizziness without features of pulmonary embolism or dissection
Not helpful unless sepsis or ischemia is suspected
Reserved for suspected meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage, not routine dizziness

decision_points: Use the HINTS exam (head impulse, nystagmus type, test of skew) in patients with acute continuous vertigo and vascular risk factors to separate peripheral from central causes
Perform the Dix-Hallpike maneuver before imaging in patients with brief positional vertigo; a positive test with typical nystagmus confirms BPPV and needs no imaging
Check orthostatic vital signs in every patient before attributing dizziness to the inner ear
Pregnancy test before CT or medication changes in anyone who could be pregnant
Sudden severe dizziness with focal deficits, new severe headache, or inability to walk needs urgent imaging rather than a vestibular suppressant

differential.name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
differential.why_considered: Brief spinning spells triggered by rolling over in bed or looking up, the most common cause of true vertigo

history: Episodes last seconds to under a minute
Triggered by specific head positions such as rolling over or bending forward
No hearing loss, tinnitus, or ear fullness
No focal neurologic symptoms
exam: Dix-Hallpike maneuver reproduces vertigo with a brief latency and upbeat-torsional nystagmus that fatigues on repeat testing
Normal cranial nerves, strength, and gait between spells
imaging: Not indicated when the Dix-Hallpike maneuver is classic and the neurologic exam is normal

differential.name: Vestibular neuritis
differential.why_considered: Sudden, continuous vertigo with nausea and unsteady gait, often after a viral illness

history: Abrupt onset of continuous vertigo lasting days
Nausea and vomiting prominent
No hearing loss
Recent upper respiratory infection
exam: Unidirectional horizontal nystagmus suppressed by visual fixation
Abnormal head impulse test with a corrective saccade on the affected side
Normal test of skew and no focal neurologic deficits
labs: Not routinely needed; glucose and basic labs to exclude mimics
imaging: MRI brain if a central cause cannot be excluded by the HINTS exam

differential.name: Posterior circulation stroke
differential.why_considered: Acute vertigo can be the presenting symptom of cerebellar or brainstem infarction
differential.trigger: Acute continuous vertigo with vascular risk factors, new severe headache, or any focal neurologic finding

history: Sudden onset of continuous vertigo
New severe headache or neck pain
Diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, or numbness
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, or atrial fibrillation
exam: Direction-changing or vertical nystagmus not suppressed by fixation
Normal head impulse test with an abnormal test of skew
Truncal ataxia or inability to sit or walk unsupported
Focal cranial nerve, motor, or sensory deficits
labs: Glucose and basic metabolic panel to exclude hypoglycemia and electrolyte causes
imaging: MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging is the preferred test and may be needed more than once if initially negative
CT head is often normal in acute posterior circulation stroke
CT angiography of the head and neck if dissection or large vessel occlusion is suspected
ecg: Atrial fibrillation or other arrhythmia suggesting a cardioembolic source

differential.name: Meniere disease
differential.why_considered: Recurrent spontaneous vertigo attacks with ear symptoms in a middle-aged adult

history: Episodes lasting 20 minutes to several hours
Unilateral fluctuating hearing loss
Tinnitus and a sense of ear fullness on the affected side
Attacks are spontaneous rather than strictly positional
exam: Asymmetric hearing on bedside screen or audiometry
Nystagmus during attacks
Normal neurologic exam between attacks
labs: Audiometry shows low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss
imaging: MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude retrocochlear pathology

differential.name: Vestibular migraine
differential.why_considered: Recurrent vertigo in a patient with a migraine history, especially a younger woman

history: Personal or family history of migraine
Episodes lasting minutes to days
Headache, photophobia, or phonophobia during or around episodes
No hearing loss
exam: Normal neurologic and vestibular examination between episodes
No positional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike
labs: Not diagnostic; used to exclude other causes
imaging: MRI brain if the presentation is atypical or red flags are present

differential.name: Orthostatic hypotension
differential.why_considered: Lightheadedness on standing is a very common cause of dizziness, especially in older adults on multiple medications

history: Symptoms occur on standing up, not with head position changes
Medications such as diuretics, alpha-blockers, or antidepressants
Diabetes with autonomic neuropathy
No true spinning sensation
exam: Drop in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mm Hg or diastolic of at least 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing, with symptoms
Heart rate rise over 30 bpm suggests volume depletion
ecg: Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia; arrhythmia may contribute

differential.name: Cardiac arrhythmia
differential.why_considered: Palpitations with lightheadedness or near-fainting suggests a cardiac cause of cerebral hypoperfusion
differential.trigger: Palpitations, syncope or near-syncope, or an irregular pulse

history: Palpitations preceding the dizziness
Near-fainting or fainting
Known heart disease or heart failure
No positional trigger
exam: Irregularly irregular pulse or bradycardia
Murmur suggesting valvular disease
Signs of heart failure
labs: Basic metabolic panel for electrolyte abnormalities
ecg: Atrial fibrillation with irregularly irregular response
Sinus bradycardia or high-grade atrioventricular block
imaging: Transthoracic echocardiogram if structural disease or a cardioembolic source is suspected

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Lightheadedness, sweating, and confusion in a patient on insulin or a sulfonylurea
differential.trigger: Diabetes on insulin or a sulfonylurea with sweating and confusion

history: Missed meal, increased activity, or excess insulin dose
Symptoms improve with eating
No true spinning vertigo
exam: Diaphoresis, tremor, confusion, or altered mental status
Symptoms resolve after glucose correction
labs: Bedside glucose below 70 mg/dL, often below 54 mg/dL with neuroglycopenic symptoms

differential.name: Anemia
differential.why_considered: Chronic lightheadedness and unsteadiness with fatigue, common in older adults

history: Gradual onset of fatigue and exertional lightheadedness
Heavy menstrual bleeding, gastrointestinal blood loss, or chronic kidney disease
No positional or spinning component
exam: Pallor, tachycardia, flow murmur
labs: Low hemoglobin; iron studies and stool testing to find the source

differential.name: Giant cell arteritis
differential.why_considered: Dizziness with headache in an older adult can signal cranial arteritis with risk of vision loss
differential.trigger: Age over 50 with new headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms

history: New headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication
Visual blurring or transient vision loss
Polymyalgia symptoms with shoulder and hip girdle pain
exam: Tender or nodular temporal artery with reduced pulsation
Visual field defect
imaging: Temporal artery biopsy is the confirmatory test; vascular ultrasound of the temporal arteries may support the diagnosis

differential.name: Medication adverse effect
differential.why_considered: Many common medications cause dizziness, especially with polypharmacy in older adults

history: Temporal link between a new or increased medication and symptoms
Antihypertensives, sedative-hypnotics, anticholinergics, or opioids
Symptoms worse after doses or on standing
exam: Orthostatic changes, sedation, or gait unsteadiness
Normal vestibular and neurologic examination
labs: Renal function to guide dose adjustment

severity.mild: Intermittent, brief episodes with no interference in daily activities; normal gait and vital signs; patient is comfortable
severity.moderate: Frequent or persistent symptoms with nausea and unsteady gait; patient avoids driving or needs to sit down; orthostatic changes may be present
severity.severe: Disabling continuous vertigo with vomiting, inability to walk without support, and dehydration; focal findings may be absent but the patient cannot function
severity.critical: Vertigo with focal neurologic deficits, inability to stand or protect the airway, or hemodynamic instability suggesting stroke, arrhythmia, or central nervous system infection

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe dizziness with weakness, numbness, slurred speech, or double vision
red_flags.meaning: Possible posterior circulation stroke; needs urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: New severe headache unlike any before, or neck pain
red_flags.meaning: Hemorrhage, dissection, or central nervous system infection

red_flags.finding: Inability to walk or stand unsupported
red_flags.meaning: Truncal ataxia suggests a central cause

red_flags.finding: Vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, or nystagmus that does not suppress with fixation
red_flags.meaning: Central rather than peripheral vestibular lesion

red_flags.finding: Fever with neck stiffness or confusion
Age over 50 with new headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms
red_flags.meaning: Giant cell arteritis with risk of permanent vision loss

red_flags.finding: Recent head trauma or anticoagulant use

complications.name: Anxiety and activity avoidance
clues: Avoidance of driving or crowded places
Persistent symptoms after the original cause resolves

complications.name: Permanent hearing loss
clues: Recurrent attacks with fluctuating hearing loss

complications.name: Stroke from missed posterior circulation ischemia

special_populations.differences: Multiple causes often coexist, including medications, orthostatic hypotension, vestibular loss, and neuropathy; falls and confusion may be the presenting complaint rather than vertigo.
Young children cannot describe spinning and present with irritability, unsteady gait, or vomiting; migraine equivalents and inner ear infections are more prominent in the differential.
Dizziness is common from physiologic changes; orthostatic hypotension, anemia, and hyperemesis must be considered, and medication choices are limited.
Autonomic neuropathy causes orthostatic dizziness, and hypoglycemia from insulin or sulfonylureas can present with lightheadedness and sweating.
Electrolyte abnormalities and medication accumulation increase dizziness; adjust doses of vestibular suppressants and avoid nephrotoxic agents.
Higher risk of central nervous system infection or malignancy presenting with dizziness, and symptoms may be blunted or atypical.

key_questions.question: When you say dizzy, do you mean the room is spinning, or that you feel lightheaded or unsteady?
key_questions.looking_for: True vertigo (spinning) points to a vestibular cause; lightheadedness or unsteadiness points to orthostasis, cardiac, metabolic, or gait causes

key_questions.question: How long does each episode last?
key_questions.looking_for: Seconds to under a minute suggests BPPV; minutes to hours suggests Meniere disease or vestibular migraine; days of continuous symptoms suggests vestibular neuritis or stroke

key_questions.question: What brings it on?
key_questions.looking_for: Rolling over in bed or looking up suggests BPPV; standing up suggests orthostatic hypotension; spontaneous onset suggests neuritis, Meniere, or migraine

key_questions.question: Did it start suddenly, and is it constant or does it come and go?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt continuous vertigo lasting days suggests vestibular neuritis or posterior circulation stroke; recurrent discrete spells suggest BPPV, Meniere, or migraine

key_questions.question: Do you have any hearing loss, ringing, or fullness in one ear?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral fluctuating hearing loss with tinnitus and fullness suggests Meniere disease; isolated hearing loss raises concern for a retrocochlear lesion

key_questions.question: Do you have a headache, and do you have a history of migraines?
key_questions.looking_for: Migraine history with recurrent vertigo episodes suggests vestibular migraine

key_questions.question: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, double vision, or trouble swallowing?
key_questions.looking_for: Focal neurologic symptoms suggest a central cause such as posterior circulation stroke

key_questions.question: Did you have a new, severe headache or neck pain with this?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests hemorrhage, vertebral artery dissection, or central nervous system infection

key_questions.question: Can you walk on your own, or do you need help?
key_questions.looking_for: Inability to stand or walk unsupported suggests truncal ataxia from a central cause

key_questions.question: Any palpitations, chest pain, or fainting?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests a cardiac arrhythmia or structural heart disease causing cerebral hypoperfusion

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent cold, flu, or ear infection?
key_questions.looking_for: A recent upper respiratory infection supports vestibular neuritis

key_questions.question: Have you had any head injury or ear surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior trauma or surgery predisposes to BPPV and other vestibular injury

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, and have any changed recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Diuretics, antihypertensives, alpha-blockers, antidepressants, sedative-hypnotics, opioids, and anticholinergics can all cause dizziness

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, and are you on insulin or a sulfonylurea?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of lightheadedness, sweating, and confusion

key_questions.question: How much are you drinking, and have you been vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor intake or vomiting suggests dehydration and orthostatic dizziness

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes the differential and the imaging and medication plan

key_questions.question: Do you drink alcohol, and how much?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy use contributes to dehydration, neuropathy, and unsteadiness

key_questions.question: Any fever, neck stiffness, or confusion?

reasoning_points: Characterize the symptom as true spinning vertigo versus lightheadedness or unsteadiness, since this drives the differential
Use episode duration and triggers to narrow the cause: seconds with position change for BPPV, minutes to hours for Meniere or migraine, days of continuous symptoms for neuritis or stroke
Ask about ear symptoms because unilateral fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and fullness point to Meniere disease
Screen for focal neurologic symptoms, new severe headache, and inability to walk, which suggest a central cause
Review medications and check orthostatic vital signs before attributing symptoms to the inner ear
Check a bedside glucose in any patient on insulin or a sulfonylurea
Use the HINTS exam in acute continuous vertigo to separate peripheral from central causes
Perform the Dix-Hallpike maneuver before imaging when the history suggests brief positional vertigo
Consider cardiac causes when palpitations, syncope, or an irregular pulse are present
Consider giant cell arteritis in an older adult with new headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms

easy: Classic BPPV: brief spinning spells triggered by rolling over in bed, positive Dix-Hallpike with fatigable upbeat-torsional nystagmus, normal neurologic exam
Clear orthostatic dizziness on standing in a patient on a diuretic, with a documented blood pressure drop
Younger patient with recurrent vertigo and a known migraine history
medium: Vestibular neuritis with days of continuous vertigo, unidirectional nystagmus suppressed by fixation, and an abnormal head impulse test
Meniere disease with fluctuating unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness between attacks
Older adult on multiple medications with overlapping orthostatic and vestibular contributions
Patient with anemia or hypothyroidism presenting with gradual unsteadiness rather than spinning
hard: Posterior circulation stroke presenting as isolated vertigo with a normal head impulse test and abnormal skew deviation
Older adult with new headache, jaw claudication, and dizziness from giant cell arteritis
Patient with hypoglycemia on insulin presenting with lightheadedness and confusion
Child who cannot describe vertigo and presents with irritability, vomiting, and unsteady gait
Persistent symptoms after the original cause resolves, with anxiety and activity avoidance
